The question that follows is who is responsible for the violations of an Autonomous Weapon System. In this paper, I focus on the challenges of accountability that are posed by AWS and the possible solutions to such. \\n\\nAWS without ‘Meaningful Human Control’ are unpredictable on the battlefield or wherever they are used.  In the event of them violating the law – violations that are not intended by the person deploying them – it is not clear who is legally responsible, thereby creating an accountability gap.  Accountability is important in international law because where there is an accountability gap; the victims’ right to a legal remedy is adversely affected.  There are four forms of accountability that I am going to discuss in this paper: individual, command, corporate and state responsibility.  Under individual and corporate responsibility, there is civil and criminal liability.\\n\\nIn summary, the arguments I make in this paper are: the above mentioned forms of accountability are complementary to each other; they are not alternatives to the exclusion of the other.  For example, if AWS create an accountability gap as far as the individual criminal responsibility of those deploying AWS on the battlefield is concerned, that specific gap is neither closed by suing the responsible individuals under civil responsibility nor holding the manufacturing company liable under corporate responsibility. \\n\\nUnder individual responsibility, as long as there remains the possibility of AWS acting in an unpredictable manner, they may present an unresolvable challenge as far as the establishment of the accused person’s mens rea is concerned. See [the reusable kernel contract](kernel.md) for application ownership and the
non-research execution proof, and [installation boundaries](installations.md) for
independent records and runtime lifecycles. These remain inside this repository.

The local [improvement application](improvements.md) uses that same kernel contract
in an explicitly new experiment record. Captured public research informs code
proposals; it does not become writable research authority. Untrusted candidate
code runs only in restricted disposable containers, while the host scores its
outputs. An operator review receipt cannot apply code or grant release authority.

The [autonomous context lane](autonomous-context.md) is a separate WAKE application
policy on the existing per-node native authority. An installed capability permits
one selector-field change, gated by recomputed fixed-task and current-native-state
measurements. Proposal generation, adoption and rollback require no per-change
human review. Metadata events preserve research versions and history; candidate
data cannot replace the evaluator, widen permissions, modify code or create a
competing research store. Native replay owns the policy after restart.

> **Current specification.** This document explains why the present system is shaped this way: its trust boundary, durable record, governance model and known limits. Current local procedures belong in `standalone.md`; public mirror publishing belongs in `cloud.md`. Maintainer navigation, environment checks and reproducible validation guidance belong in `development.md`.

**WAKE✳︎** is infrastructure for continuity of accountable work, not continuity of a model instance. Its stable sequence is **Record → Context → Proposal → Governance → Transition → Receipt**.
